title: Stable rotating vortex clusters in three-dimensional quantum droplets
abstract: We predict a new type of stable three-dimensional (3D) vortex quantum droplets in binary Bose-Einstein condensate arranged into ring clusters that per-sistently rotate in the external potential. In contrast to clusters composed from localized quantum droplets, the states introduced here represent interacting vortex lines with identical topological charges nested in common 3D envelope and existing in much broader parameter range in comparison with local-ized quantum droplets. The intricate interplay between mean-field nonlinearity of Bose-Einstein condensate, quantum fluctuations described by Lee-Huang-Yang correction, Coriolis force arising due to rotation, and external potential leads to substantial variations of cluster shape upon increase of its rotation frequency. Rotating vortex clusters bifurcate from single-vortex quantum droplets and exist only above critical value of the rotation frequency that decreases with increase of chemical potential and depends on the number of vortex lines in the cluster. The radius of the cluster decreases with increase of rotation frequency and weakly varies with chemical potential, which determines mostly localization of the individual vortices in cluster and overall width of its envelope. Vortex droplet clusters are very robust objects existing in stable form in wide intervals of the number of particles for any number (odd or even) of vortex lines forming them. Our results may open the route to observation of stable arrays of vortex lines of different configurations per-forming regular collective motion in condensate.
summary: This paper predicts the existence of stable, rotating three-dimensional vortex quantum droplets within binary Bose-Einstein condensates. These clusters are stabilized by a combination of mean-field interactions, quantum fluctuations, and the Coriolis force due to rotation. The findings open theoretical avenues for observing stable, collective motion of multiple vortex lines in ultracold atomic systems.
main_problem: The paper predicts and characterizes stable three-dimensional (3D) vortex quantum droplets formed in binary Bose-Einstein condensates (BEC) that exhibit persistent rotation.
main_result: Stable vortex clusters, distinct from localized droplets, are found to exist in a wide parameter range, suggesting a route to observing regular collective motion of vortex lines in condensates.
method: The study involves solving coupled dimensionless Gross-Pitaevskii equations incorporating Lee-Huang-Yang (LHY) quantum corrections and the Coriolis force arising from rotation.
model_or_system: The system is a binary Bose-Einstein condensate modeled in 3D geometry, analyzed under the influence of mean-field nonlinearity, quantum fluctuations (LHY), rotation, and an external potential.
key_observables: The norm ($N$) of the cluster, the cluster radius, the distance between adjacent vortices, and the critical rotation frequency ($\omega_{crit}$).
important_parameters: Chemical potential ($\mu$), rotation frequency ($\omega$), and the number of vortex lines ($n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes equal masses and intra-species interactions for simplicity, and the stability is critically dependent on the repulsive LHY quantum corrections balancing the attractive residual mean-field nonlinearity.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the dependence of the cluster norm ($N$) on chemical potential ($\mu$) for 2, 3, and 4 vortex lines, illustrating bifurcation from single-vortex states. Other figures show 3D isosurfaces and stability evolution.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical model and governing equations, predicting the existence of the new cluster type, analyzing the dependence of cluster properties (size, norm) on rotation frequency and chemical potential, and finally demonstrating stability through numerical simulations.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the complex dynamics of interacting quantum fluids, specifically exploring how external forces (rotation) and quantum corrections stabilize exotic topological structures (vortex clusters) in BECs.
